title: Conditional Associations Between HEXACO Personality Traits and NEET Status in Young Adults
description:
Young people classified as NEET (Not in Employment, Education, or Training) represent a heterogeneous population whose educational and occupational disengagement may be shaped by the interplay between personality traits, psychological resources, and contextual conditions. Although previous research has examined several risk factors associated with NEET status, evidence on the role of personality and its interaction with self-regulatory and psychosocial resources remains limited. 

This study examined the psychological and sociodemographic correlates of NEET status in a sample of 254 young adults, including 75 NEET and 179 non-NEET participants. HEXACO personality dimensions, perceived employability, self-directed learning, future-oriented beliefs, mental health, perceived social support, education, age, and sex were assessed. Principal component analysis identified three broader dimensions: Strategic Future-Oriented Mindset, Mental Health, and Social Support. A binomial regression model showed that NEET status was associated with a complex pattern of conditional effects rather than with isolated personality traits. Strategic Future-Oriented Mindset was negatively associated with NEET status particularly at low and average levels of Honesty–Humility. Social Support was associated with a lower probability of being NEET mainly among individuals high in Extraversion. Emotionality emerged as the most stable personality-related risk factor, whereas education was negatively associated with NEET status and moderated the role of specific personality dimensions. 

These findings suggest that NEET status should be understood through a person-context framework in which personality traits interact with psychological resources and sociodemographic conditions. title: Dialogical Emergence in Embodied Collaboration: A Micro-Analysis of How Dyads Co-Construct Insight from Conflicting Perceptions
description:
In real-time embodied collaboration, partners occupying distinct vantage points capture only local projections of the system state. When these projections conflict—for instance, when one partner perceives “pushing” while the other perceives “being pulled”—both may mistake locally valid experience for complete truth, falling into a structural illusion. Whether and how collaborators can transcend these perspectival limits through dialogue, when physical repositioning and direct perceptual sharing are infeasible, remains theoretically under-addressed.
Using partnered dance as a model system, this multi-case qualitative study recruited four established dyads who completed a standardized task and participated in dyadic synchronized video-stimulated recall interviews. Grounded in a phenomenologically-dialogical epistemology, we employed a three-tiered analytical framework—thematic content, interaction process, and identity-narrative analysis—to analyze approximately 320 minutes of recorded interview data, with segments containing perceptual divergence (totaling ~58 minutes across 16 segments) subjected to full micro-level dialogical coding.
Four major findings emerged. First, perceptual divergence reflects each partner conflating a local projection with a complete system description, signaling temporary breakdown of pre-reflective intercorporeality. Second, partners exhibited two qualitatively distinct pathways: adversarial persistence, where dialogue stagnated in repetitive cycles of negation, and integrative co-construction, where partners collaboratively discovered the partiality of their perceptions and generated emergent understanding. Third, integrative co-construction followed a recurrent six-phase micro-structure: Divergence Exposure, Pause-and-Inquiry, Individual Retrospection, Difference Localization, Emergent Reframing, and New Consensus Formation. title: Revisiting Long-Term Trends in Germany’s Upper Secondary Mathematics Achievement:  A Chain Linking Analysis from FIMS 1964 to TIMSS 1996
description:
Public discourse in many countries reflects a persistent perception of declining educational achievement over the decades, particularly among upper secondary graduates in mathematics at the transition to higher education. Assessing such claims requires evidence of long-term trends. International large-scale assessments (ILSAs), including earlier study cycles, provide a key data source, especially where systematic monitoring is lacking. In Germany, participation in ILSAs has been discontinuous and upper secondary monitoring is absent. However, data from the First International Mathematics Study (FIMS, 1964) and the Third International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS, 1996) allow the reconstruction of achievement trends over more than three decades. This study therefore estimates trends in mathematics achievement among German upper secondary graduates between 1964 and 1996 through a secondary analysis of these data.
Item response theory was used to rescale the achievement data. FIMS Germany and TIMSS Germany were chain linked via Sweden across FIMS, the Second International Mathematics Study (SIMS, 1980-82), and TIMSS using Haberman linking. Subsequently, achievement distributions for 1964 and 1996 were transformed onto the TIMSS trend scale. Sampling and linking errors were computed to assess uncertainty.
The results indicate a non-significant gain of 22 points in achievement between 1964 and 1996. Subgroup analyses reveal a significant increase in achievement for students enrolled in advanced mathematics courses, whereas no significant changes are observed for basic course levels. The decomposition of uncertainty shows that linking error substantially exceeds sampling error, indicating that trend estimates are primarily driven by item-related uncertainty. At the same time, linking error was reduced relative to a previously reported joint linking approach.
